This is f*cking insane.

Chinese researchers just dropped a paper with a title that will make every agent framework nervous: "The End of Harness Engineering".

The argument fits in one line: writing the program around the model is finished as a skill.

A harness written by a human is one person's guess about one task on one afternoon. It ships, nobody re-reads it, nobody scores it, and the agent runs that guess for months.

A harness written by the loop is a file that grades itself. A small 4B model reads what failed, writes 8 edits, and only the edit that scores best on held-out questions survives.

The big model never changes. The file around it does, every round.

So the human job collapses to one artifact: the scoring set. You write the questions, never the program.

Frameworks turn disposable. The exam turns into the job.

That is the exact loop I built and documented below: one https://t.co/JlQQhqH44N, 300 Kimi K3 workers, 37 rewrites in 41 rounds, zero opened by me.

The whole paper in one line: write the exam before the code ↓

hits.text:
A construction firm wired Opus 5.5 into its modelling workflow, and the buildings started failing review less than the ones drafted by hand

Nothing about the drawings looked different. What changed is that the model knows a building has to be assembled, not just drawn.

> DRAFT - the structure modelled from the brief with real materials and real spans
> CLASH - every system checked against the others before anything reaches a drawing set
> CODE - clearances, egress and loads validated against the rules that apply to the site
> BUILD - the sequence checked, so nothing is designed in a place it cannot be installed

Clash detection already exists. It runs at the end, which is exactly when a conflict is most expensive to resolve.

Here it runs while the geometry is still soft. A pipe crossing a beam gets moved before anyone has drawn the beam’s details.

The sequencing check is the one nobody automates. A perfect design can still be impossible to assemble in order.

Code compliance is where hand-drafting quietly leaks time. One missed clearance sends a full set back weeks.

The model does not design the building. It catches the conflicts a person only finds after the drawings are finished.

Review cycles went from several rounds to barely more than one, and that is the whole saving.

The workflow, the clash log and a full validated set are laid out underneath.

It is becoming f*cking dangerous: The engineer behind Claude Code just advised users to wipe their CLAUDE.md file completely

This is not a joke

Boris Cherny, at YC: "Every six months, completely clear out your CLAUDE.md, strip away your custom skills, and remove your hooks. Let the model run fresh and you might be amazed by what happens"

The logic behind it:

Your previous prompt rules were written to cover up flaws in older system versions

Fresh model releases no longer suffer from those exact limitations

Keeping those legacy prompts around might actually degrade Claude's output quality today

The step by step process:

1. Erase CLAUDE.md, along with all integrated skills and hooks
2. Go about your normal workflow and spot where the AI starts to drift off course
3. Bring back a single rule only when you notice a specific error recurring over and over
4. Execute this reset whenever a major model upgrade drops

Things to keep:

Essential safety protocols and strict compliance guidelines

Non-obvious project quirks that cannot be inferred directly from reading code

Things to trash:

Directory layouts, lists of packages, and high-level architecture breakdowns

Any information the AI can figure out on its own by analyzing your codebase

While most developers keep adding more and more constraints, the creator of the tool is doing the exact opposite by cutting them down

Add this to your bookmarks. I'm sure you're hearing about this for the first time

Anthropic builder shipped a full sandbox world on Fable 5.1 alone, and the team it replaced was eleven people

Not a demo scene. Terrain, props, interiors, interactions, all of it generated and all of it holding together as one place.

> SEED - the world described once, then expanded into regions with their own rules
> GROW - every asset generated against those rules instead of pulled from a library
> BIND - interactions written alongside the geometry, so nothing is decorative by accident

A sandbox dies on inconsistency. One building that cannot be entered teaches the player to stop trying doors.

It is becoming f*cking dangerous: AI agents mapped out a full codebase based on just one question

Jev creator Diogo Almeida put together a playbook to sync up 80 agents over 540,000 lines of code, creating a visual flow of the system architecture

Simply ask: "What takes place when a user uploads a file?" and follow the full circuit from the frontend and API down to background jobs, databases, and tests

Every element on the layout connects straight to the underlying codebase.

Claude Code agents map out the underlying code. Jev directs tasks to the right workers and strips away irrelevant data for each investigation phase:

> which specific component handles this functionality
> which files need to be analyzed
> is another worker currently handling this route
> does this part require a deeper look

The final blueprint charted 170 user flows and tied them to 2,400 tests. On top of that, 26 open points remained clearly flagged for manual review

How to use it:

Hand over the playbook along with your repo to Claude Code, then submit this prompt:

Generate a searchable blueprint of this repository

Run an audit on entry points, services, background tasks, and databases. Assign separate modules to different agents

Map every user scenario through the codebase. Link file locations and key references to each step

Rely on Jev to manage the workflow and filter out context noise. Set up dedicated agents to double-check proposed links against the raw code

Connect existing tests to their respective flows. Flag assumed logic and incomplete paths, then build a UI to navigate the map

A good approach is to run a trial on a single user path first before scaling it up to the full repository

This way, any incoming developer can review a feature, trace its dependencies, and locate test cases prior to making a single change

It's called Headroom, and it might be the smartest fix to high token usage

Your agent reads a 10,000-token log file to find one error.
You paid for all 10,000 tokens.
The answer needed 1,200.

Headroom sits between your agent and the LLM and compresses everything before the model sees it.

JSON, code, logs, RAG chunks, each gets its own specialized compressor.

And it's reversible: the originals stay on your machine, so nothing is lost.

The results speak for themselves:

→ Up to 95% fewer tokens
→ Same accuracy on benchmarks
→ Zero changes to your code

Setup takes one minute:

1. pip install "headroom-ai[all]"
2. headroom wrap claude

Done.

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and anything OpenAI-compatible.

Everything runs locally, fully open source.

The cheapest token is the one you never send.

🔗 Github repo: https://t.co/SSMujMiwMy

So, are you compressing your context, or just paying the bill?

→ Up to 95% fewer tokens
→ Same accuracy on benchmarks
→ Zero changes to your code

2. headroom wrap claude

Done.

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and anything OpenAI-compatible.

Everything runs locally, fully open source.

The cheapest token is the one you never send.
